## Part 2 - Construction of three different decision trees
For the second part of the lab we fit three separate decision trees:

### Decision tree with default settings
\
```{r fit1}
```

The default settings tree has the following misclassification rates for
training and validation data.

```{r fit1-miss, echo=FALSE}
```

### Decision tree with smallest allowed node size equal to 7000
\
```{r fit2}
```

With a smallest allowed node size of 7000 the decision tree gets smaller (One
less branch). This is because the smallest allowed node size controls how many
observations are required in a leaf for a split to be allowed to happen. In the
following table we can see the number of observations per leaf of the tree.
```{r, echo=FALSE}
table(fit2$where)
```
Only "leaf 6" could potentially split into more branches (but does not due to
other factors in the tree).

The minimum node size tree has the following misclassification rates for
training and validation data.

```{r fit2-miss, echo=FALSE}
```

### Decision tree with minimum deviance 0.0005
\
```{r fit3}
```

With a minimum deviance of 0.0005 a split must achieve a 0.05% reduction in
deviance in order to be allowed (compared to the 1% reduction required by the
default settings). A minimum deviance of 0.0005 allows the tree to grow much 
larger, as illustrated by the plot of our third tree, which shows a significant
increase in size compared to previous trees.

The tree with minimum deviance 0.0005 has the following misclassification rates 
for training and validation data.

```{r fit3-miss, echo=FALSE}
```

### Best decision tree

```{r echo=FALSE}
data.frame(
  row.names=c("Training misclassification", "Validation misclassification"),
  DefaultTree=c(fit1_training_miss, fit1_validation_miss),
  MinSizeTree=c(fit2_training_miss, fit2_validation_miss),
  MinDevTree=c(fit3_training_miss, fit3_validation_miss)
)
```

Looking at the training and validation data misclassification rates for our 
three decision trees we can see that the lowest training misclassification
happens in the third tree with 9.4% misclassification. The same tree also has
the highest validation misclassification which indicates overfitting.

The first and second decision trees have both identical training and validation
misclassification. In this case a simpler/smaller tree is usually better as they
are easier to interpret and are less likely to overfit to unseen data. For this
reason the best decision tree is the minsize=7000 tree (the second tree).


## Part 3 - Find optimal tree depth for min deviance 0.0005 tree
To find the optimal tree depth for our fit3 tree we prune the tree to
all possible amounts of leaves between 2 and 50. For each tree we record
its deviance for the training and validation data. This gives the
following plot of the dependence of deviances for the training and
validation data on the number of leaves.

```{r part3, echo=FALSE}
```

From the plot we see the deviance of the training data is always
decreasing with more leaves. The deviance for the test data decreases
until around 20 leaves whereafter it gets unstable. This is due to the
decision tree overfitting to the training data at higher amounts of
leaves. The optimal amount of leaves is gotten as follows:

```{r opt-leaves}
```

With the optimal amount of leaves we create a optimal tree from fit3
with 22 leaves.

```{r opt-tree, echo=FALSE}
```

From the decision tree we can see that the most important variable for
decision making is the outcome of previous campaigns towards a specific
customer (poutcome).

A less expected variable that is shown to be quite important in the decision
tree is the current month during a campaign. During the months of Mars, September,
October and December we always predict "no" (depending on the outcome of first 
branch). Month continues to appear in branches further down the tree which 
indicates that the time of year during a campaign is relevant in all levels of
prediction.

Another variable that shows up early and multiple times throughout the tree is 
"pdays" which represents the number of days since last attempted campaign
towards a specific customer. In the right branch (from root node) we can see that
no matter how many days its been since last attempted campaign we predict "yes"
if the previous campaign succeeded.

In the left branch (from root node) the majority of outcomes result in "no". 
There is a single leaf resulting in "yes" when the contact is "known" and 
"pdays >= 383" since last contact. This could be interpreted as a
new customers that is now receiving their first campaign call.

## Part 4 - Statistics of optimal tree
```{r part4-conf, echo=FALSE}
```

From the confusion matrix of the optimal tree we calculate the accuracy
and F1-score.

```{r part4-acc, echo=FALSE}
```

This gives us a total misclassification of only about 10% which might
appear good but in our data set the majority of outcomes result in "no"
with few "yes". This means it might be more appropriate to use F1-score
as a measure for predictive power to make sure the model is also good at
predicted the less common outcomes.

```{r part4-f1, echo=FALSE}
```

The F1-score is very low which indicates that the decision tree is not
very good at predicting cases of "yes". For our tree the F1-score should
be the preferred as the data set is unbalanced.

## Part 5 - Decision tree classification with loss matrix
When applying the loss matrix given in the lab instructions to the
predictions of the optimal tree we get the following confusion matrix:

```{r part5, echo=FALSE}
```

From this confusion matrix we calculate the accuracy and F1-score again.

```{r part5-acc, echo=FALSE}
```

```{r part5-f1, echo=FALSE}
```

In the classification with the loss matrix the accuracy is slightly
lower (87.3% compared to 89.2%) but the F1-score is substantially better
(48.6% compared to 28.5%).

With the loss matrix the decision tree will try harder to predict "yes"
correctly at the cost of slightly lower accuracy. Our data set is
unbalanced which makes the F1-score a more important statistic to
optimize for.

## Part 6 - Compute TPR and FPR for a logistic regression model and decision tree
In the last part of the lab we compare the classification performance
between the optimal tree and a logistic regression model using the
following principle.
$\hat{Y} = \text{yes if } p(Y=\text{'yes'} \mid X) > \pi,\ \text{otherwise } \hat{Y} = \text{no}$
where $\pi$ = 0.05,0.1,0.15, … 0.9,0.95.

For each value of $\pi$ we calculate the true positive rate (TPR) and
false positive rate (FPR) for both models. Lastly all values are
inserted into a plot.

```{r part6, echo=FALSE}
```

Both the decision tree and logistic regression have very similar
ROC-curves. The decision tree curve is after FPR=0.6 consistently very
slightly above the logistic regression curve. From these plots the
performance of the two models appear to be almost equal.

A precision-recall curve is better at showing performance on predictions
on the positive outcomes of a model. As previously stated our data set
is unbalanced with the majority of outcomes being "no". This means a PR
curve could be more appropriate, just as F1-score is more appropriate
than accuracy for our decision trees.
